intro: Tangier's best-known tree stands in the Mendoubia gardens beside the Grand Socco: a Moreton Bay fig whose buttress roots run out across the lawn in front of the old residency of the Mendoub. Guides and signs call it 800 years old. A reader who sent us its photograph puts it at 120 to 140, planted around 1900, since the species came from Australia. Free, in a public park on the edge of the medina.
meta_description: The Moreton Bay fig of the Mendoubia gardens in Tangier: huge buttress roots, a public park by the Grand Socco, and an age legend a reader corrects.

trees.name: The Moreton Bay Fig of the Mendoubia
trees.age_estimate: 120 to 140 years by a reader's estimate; guides and signs say 800 to 1,000

location.address: Jardin de la Mendoubia, beside the Grand Socco (Place du 9 Avril 1947), Tangier

trees.story:
Guides and park signs in Tangier call this tree 800 or even 1,000 years old. The reader who sent us its photograph disagrees, and puts the case in one line: that age “predates the historical introduction of Australian flora to the Mediterranean basin by several centuries.” The Moreton Bay fig, Ficus macrophylla, comes from the coastal rainforests of eastern Australia. In the reader’s account this one was planted between the 1880s and 1900s, beside the residency of the Mendoub, the Sultan’s representative to Tangier’s international administration. That makes it roughly 120 to 140 years old, by a reader’s estimate.

Young, then, next to the legend, and still enormous. The photograph shows the trunk opening at its foot into wide, plank-like roots that run out across the grass, under a dark evergreen crown that shades the lawn and the white walls of the Mendoubia behind it. The reader gives the trunk as about 2.2 to 2.8 metres across, with the root flare more than 10 metres around.

In their words, the tree “survived the transformation of the site from administrative grounds and adjacent cemeteries into the public city park that stands today.” That park is the Mendoubia gardens, beside the Grand Socco. Wikipedia’s page on the Mendoubia mentions a large tree in the grounds said to be 800 years old, which is the figure the reader set out to correct.

If you go, a tape around the trunk would settle the girth.
trees.how_to_recognise: A huge fig whose trunk opens at the foot into wide, plank-like buttress roots running out over the lawn, in front of the white Mendoubia building with its green-framed arched windows.
trees.verify_notes: 2026-10-21: published from a reader's app photograph and note (sighting 2aa7147b, GPS fix taken at the tree on 2026-10-18) on Hidde's 2026-10-21 ruling: a good reader photograph with a GPS fix goes live, focus areas or not (Morocco was out of focus as Africa); the reader's words go on the page. Species, planting window (1880s to 1900s), age (120 to 140) and trunk measures are the reader's, stated as theirs. Wikipedia's Mendoubia page confirms a large old tree in the grounds, which it calls a banyan said to be 800 years old; the reader's note says that figure is a myth repeated by guides and signage. No register, no girth tape.
trees.access: Free, in a public city park beside the Grand Socco, open in daytime.
trees.transport: In the centre of Tangier, on the edge of the medina at the Grand Socco; a walk from most of the old town, and by petit taxi from Tanger Ville station.

question_meta: Tangier's famous Mendoubia fig is a Moreton Bay fig, about 120 to 140 years old by a reader's estimate, not 800. Where it stands and how to see it.
question_answer: The best-known old tree in Tangier is the Moreton Bay fig (Ficus macrophylla) in the Mendoubia gardens, beside the Grand Socco on the edge of the medina. Guides and park signs often give it 800 to 1,000 years; a reader who photographed it for us puts it at about 120 to 140, planted between the 1880s and 1900s beside the residency of the Mendoub. It is free to see, in a public park open in daytime.
question_context: The age is disputed, and neither figure comes from a ring count or a register. Wikipedia's page on the Mendoubia mentions a large tree in the grounds said to be 800 years old, and guides and park signs repeat 800 to 1,000. The reader who photographed it for us argues from the species: the Moreton Bay fig is native to the subtropical coastal rainforests of eastern Australia and reached North Africa in the late nineteenth century, so a claim of 800 years would predate its arrival by centuries. In their account the tree was planted between the 1880s and 1900s, during Tangier's diplomatic expansion, next to the residency of the Mendoub, the Sultan's representative to the city's international administration. The grounds later changed from administrative land and neighbouring cemeteries into the public park that is there today, and the fig came through that change. The reader describes wide, plank-like buttress roots, spreading branches that let down aerial roots, a trunk about 2.2 to 2.8 metres across and a root flare of more than 10 metres around. Nobody has published a tape measurement.
